questions.question: Explain how anaesthetics solved the problem of pain in surgery.
questions.expected_answer: Before the eighteen-forties, patients were awake during operations, given only alcohol or opium and held down, so many died of shock and surgeons worked very fast. In 1846, William Morton gave a patient ether in Boston and a lump was removed painlessly. In 1847, James Simpson found chloroform worked and was easier to use, and Queen Victoria's use of it in childbirth in 1853 helped people accept anaesthetics. Early anaesthetics had dangers, but safer methods followed.

questions.question: How did Joseph Lister and Karl Landsteiner make surgery safer?
questions.expected_answer: Many patients died of infection after surgery because surgeons did not clean hands or instruments. Inspired by Pasteur's germ discovery, Lister began in 1865 to use carbolic acid to clean wounds, dressings and instruments and sprayed it during operations, and deaths fell sharply; later aseptic surgery kept germs out with sterilised instruments, gowns, masks and gloves. Landsteiner discovered blood groups in 1901, showing transfusions are safe only when groups match, which led to blood banks.

questions.question: Describe the discovery of X-rays and its importance.
questions.expected_answer: In November 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen discovered invisible rays that pass through flesh but not bone or metal, and called them X-rays because X means unknown; an early picture showed his wife's hand bones and ring. Within months, hospitals used X-rays to find broken bones and objects, and army doctors used them to find bullets, including in the South African War. Röntgen won the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901, and South African Allan Cormack later helped develop CT scanning.
